from pypdf import PdfReader
from pathlib import Path
r = PdfReader('manuscript.pdf')
print('PAGES:',len(r.pages))
print('METADATA:',r.metadata)
texts=[]
for i,p in enumerate(r.pages,1):

 texts.append(f'\\n\\n=== PAGE {i} ===\\n{t}')
Path('tmp/pdfs/manuscript.txt').write_text(''.join(texts))
print(''.join(texts[:3]))
PY"

strengths: AVIS is a meaningful task formulation that combines sound-source identification, instance segmentation, and temporal identity tracking. Distinguishing sounding instances of the same category extends the capabilities of audio-visual saliency and semantic segmentation. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-01/reviews/b03/review-experiment-_fs4epdw/call-0e8a5435ad6c4de895bf7fc2ab466308/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The annotation effort provides a concrete starting point: 117 annotated videos contain 6,973 frames, 281 objects, and 15,355 masks. The broader collection spans 26 categories and five scenarios, with substantially longer videos than the cited AVSBench setting.

The baseline sensibly combines established Mask2Former and audio-visual fusion components. Table 1 supplies initial reference results of 31.5 AP with ResNet-50 and 35.6 AP with Swin-Base. The explicitly defined video-level IoU and standard VIS AP/AR metrics appropriately account for segmentation and temporal consistency.

The task distinctions are clearly illustrated, and the manuscript reports useful implementation details, including optimization settings, training iterations, batch size, frame sampling, and hardware.
weaknesses: The central audio-dependent behavior is not established. Table 1 compares only visual backbones; there is no visual-only Mask2Former baseline or muted/shuffled-audio control. Consequently, the results cannot distinguish successful use of audio from recognition of visually likely sound sources. Ablations also do not establish the contributions of TPAVI and audio-conditioned queries. This missing validation is a decisive concern for the proposed task and benchmark.

The annotation protocol does not substantiate the claimed label quality. Section 3 identifies a SAM-based labeling tool but does not explain how annotators determine which individual objects are audible during overlapping sounds, handle silent intervals, preserve identities across interruptions, or verify annotations. These decisions define the ground truth for AVIS; mask-generation assistance alone does not establish their reliability.

The evaluated benchmark is much narrower than the collected corpus: only 117 of 1,258 videos are annotated, with 84 training and 33 testing videos. The manuscript does not report category coverage within these splits or the prevalence of simultaneous and same-category sound sources. Figure 3 describes the broader collection, so it cannot establish the diversity of the actual evaluation. Dataset size alone is not disqualifying, but these omissions leave the benchmark's distinguishing challenges insufficiently characterized.

Important implementation details remain ambiguous. Section 4.2 does not explain how the time-indexed learned instance queries support variable-length inference after two-frame training. Equation (1) leaves the contraction and projection dimensions needed for its residual addition unspecified. Audio-window alignment is also unclear, and the manuscript provides no dataset or implementation access link. These are reproducibility gaps, rather than demonstrated proof that the model is incorrect.

The methodological originality is limited: the architecture primarily integrates existing segmentation and fusion components. That is reasonable for an introductory benchmark baseline, but it places greater weight on establishing the dataset's validity and audio-specific usefulness. The useful task formulation and initial annotations do not currently outweigh the missing evidence on those central points.
